The Arctic Imperative: Why the United States Must Pursue Greenland

A Strategic Acquisition Whose Time Has Come

The debate surrounding American interest in Greenland is often dismissed as geopolitical fantasy or diplomatic recklessness, a talking point mocked in polished editorial rooms and European foreign ministries alike. This dismissiveness is a strategic error. Behind the awkward optics and the inevitable controversy lies a genuinely compelling case — one grounded in military necessity, resource reality, great power competition, and a historical tradition of American territorial expansion that has consistently proven, with the benefit of hindsight, to have been visionary rather than imperialist. The United States should pursue the acquisition of Greenland through persistent, serious, well-resourced diplomatic and economic engagement, and it should do so with urgency, because the window for doing so on favorable terms is narrowing with every passing year.

This essay will make that case plainly and thoroughly. It will acknowledge the legitimate objections — the concerns of Greenlanders, the sensitivities of the Danish government, the international legal complexities — and argue that each of these obstacles, real as they are, is surmountable and that the strategic logic of acquisition ultimately outweighs them. The United States has always shaped its geography to serve its security. Greenland is the next chapter in that tradition.

I. The Historical Precedent Is Overwhelming

American territorial expansion has never been polite. The Louisiana Purchase was negotiated with a Napoleon who had no particularly clean title to the land. The acquisition of Florida required sustained pressure on Spain. Alaska was purchased from Russia in 1867 amid widespread ridicule — "Seward's Folly," the newspapers called it — and proved to be among the most consequential land deals in the nation's history. The United States has purchased territory, annexed territory, and on several occasions simply taken territory when its strategic interests demanded it.

Greenland itself has been on the American radar since at least 1867, when Secretary of State William Seward floated the idea alongside his Alaska purchase. President Truman offered Denmark $100 million in gold for the island in 1946. This was not considered scandalous at the time — it was considered sensible statecraft. The offer was rejected, but the American interest was entirely legitimate, rooted in the freshly demonstrated strategic value of Arctic geography during the Second World War.

The United States already maintains Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base) in northern Greenland under a 1951 defense agreement, which means American strategic infrastructure is already embedded in the island. The question is not whether America has interests in Greenland — it unambiguously does — but whether formalized sovereignty would better serve those interests than the current ambiguous arrangement. History suggests that full sovereign control of strategically critical geography is almost always preferable to dependency on a third-party ally's goodwill, however close that ally may be.

II. The Arctic Is the Next Great Theater of Competition

To understand why Greenland matters so profoundly, one must understand what is happening in the Arctic. Climate change, whatever one thinks of its causes and consequences, is physically transforming the high north in ways that have concrete geopolitical implications. The Arctic Ocean is becoming navigable. Sea routes that were previously inaccessible for significant portions of the year are opening. The Northwest Passage, which runs through Canadian Arctic waters, and the Northern Sea Route, which Russia claims as internal waters along its northern coast, are emerging as viable commercial shipping lanes that could fundamentally reshape global trade patterns.

Greenland sits at the geographic center of this transformation. It occupies approximately 836,000 square miles — roughly three times the size of Texas — and its position between the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans makes it one of the most strategically located landmasses on earth. Control of Greenland means influence over the GIUK Gap — the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom Gap — which is the critical choke point through which Russian naval vessels must pass to reach the North Atlantic. During the Cold War, this gap was the central theater of the anti-submarine warfare competition between NATO and the Soviet Union. It remains critical today as Russian submarine activity in the North Atlantic has returned to Cold War levels and is accelerating.

The United States, for all its military power, has limited Arctic infrastructure. Russia has invested massively in its Arctic presence: dozens of Arctic military bases, the world's largest fleet of icebreakers, a dedicated Arctic military command, and a declared strategy of Arctic dominance. China, though not an Arctic nation, has declared itself a "near-Arctic state" and is aggressively pursuing Arctic shipping, resource development, and scientific research. China has repeatedly sought to invest in Greenlandic infrastructure — airports, ports, mining operations — and has been rebuffed only through concerted pressure from the United States and Denmark.

This is precisely the problem. The United States currently relies on Danish goodwill and NATO obligations to prevent Chinese and Russian strategic encroachment on Greenland. Denmark is a small country with a defense budget of approximately 2% of GDP and no meaningful Arctic military capacity of its own. It is, in the most straightforward terms, not equipped to defend or develop Greenland as a strategic asset. The United States, if it possessed sovereignty over Greenland, would be.

III. The Resource Argument Is Not Greed — It Is Necessity

Critics of American interest in Greenland frequently characterize the resource argument as naked corporate greed dressed up in strategic language. This characterization is superficially clever and substantively wrong. The resource question is genuinely a matter of national security, and here is why.

Greenland's subsoil contains some of the world's largest known deposits of rare earth elements — the minerals essential for the production of electric vehicle batteries, wind turbines, fighter jet components, missile guidance systems, semiconductors, and virtually every technology that will define both the clean energy transition and the military competition of the 21st century. The United States currently depends on China for approximately 80% of its rare earth imports. This is a strategic vulnerability of the first order. China has already demonstrated its willingness to weaponize rare earth supply chains — it cut off rare earth exports to Japan during a territorial dispute in 2010 — and any serious conflict with China would immediately expose this dependence as catastrophic.

Greenland's rare earth deposits, particularly the Kvanefjeld deposit in southern Greenland, are among the largest on earth. Development of these resources would not merely enrich investors; it would structurally reduce American dependence on Chinese supply chains in a sector where that dependence poses existential security risks. Beyond rare earths, Greenland possesses substantial reserves of oil, natural gas, zinc, lead, gold, and uranium. The United States Geological Survey estimates that the waters around Greenland may contain as much as 17% of the world's undiscovered oil and 30% of its undiscovered natural gas.

None of this is an argument for reckless resource extraction. A sovereign United States government would have every interest in developing these resources responsibly, in partnership with Greenlandic communities, with appropriate environmental protections, and in ways consistent with the island's own development priorities. But the current arrangement — in which these resources sit largely undeveloped while China courts Greenlandic politicians and Danish administrators nervously watch — serves no one's long-term interests, including Greenland's.

IV. Greenland's Own Political Trajectory Points Toward a Transition

A common objection to American acquisition of Greenland frames it as the imposition of one colonizer replacing another — the United States simply muscling in on Danish territory without regard for Greenlandic self-determination. This objection has emotional and rhetorical force, but it obscures the actual political situation on the island.

Greenland is not a content Danish province. It is a self-governing territory with its own parliament, the Inatsisartut, its own government, and a declared aspiration for full independence. The majority of Greenlandic political parties support independence from Denmark, and this aspiration has been openly expressed for decades. The 2009 Self-Government Act granted Greenland extensive autonomy and explicitly acknowledged the right of Greenlanders to pursue full independence. Greenland is, in a meaningful sense, already in the process of leaving Denmark. The question is not whether Greenland will eventually separate from the Kingdom of Denmark, but what it will become when it does.

An independent Greenland of 56,000 people, geographically enormous but economically underdeveloped, sitting between the world's most powerful military forces and subject to economic and political pressure from Russia and China, would face extraordinary vulnerabilities. Currently, Greenland receives approximately half a billion dollars annually in subsidies from Denmark — roughly $9,000 per person — and its economy has limited capacity to replace this support without either exploitation of its natural resources or substantial external partnership.

The United States could offer a genuinely compelling alternative: full respect for Greenlandic cultural identity and governance, robust investment in Greenlandic economic development, co-management of natural resource extraction with substantial revenue sharing, and the security guarantee of American sovereignty and military protection. This would not require erasing Greenlandic identity — Puerto Rico, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and other American territories maintain distinct cultural identities within the American constitutional framework. Indeed, the negotiation could structure Greenland with a degree of autonomy comparable to or greater than what it currently enjoys under Danish self-governance.

A persuasion-based, economically generous, Greenland-centered negotiation is not colonialism. It is the kind of complicated, interest-balancing diplomacy that has characterized successful territorial transitions throughout American history. The key is that it must be conducted with genuine respect for Greenlandic voices and genuine responsiveness to Greenlandic priorities — not as an afterthought, but as the central organizing principle of any negotiation.

V. The NATO and Alliance Argument Cuts Both Ways

Critics frequently argue that American pursuit of Greenland would damage NATO solidarity and alienate Denmark, undermining the alliance structures that undergird American security. This is a serious concern that deserves serious engagement. But the argument cuts in both directions.

Yes, aggressive or contemptuous American pursuit of Greenland — the kind that treats Danish sovereignty with disdain and ignores Greenlandic opinions — would damage alliance relationships. This is why the method matters enormously. But the underlying strategic argument is one that many NATO allies, if they are being honest, privately understand. Denmark's capacity to defend and develop Greenland as the Arctic becomes increasingly contested is simply inadequate to the task. The rest of the alliance recognizes this, even if diplomatic courtesy prevents them from saying so publicly.

Moreover, the alliance itself would benefit from American sovereignty over Greenland in concrete ways. American control of Greenland would close one of the most significant vulnerabilities in NATO's Arctic posture. It would provide the alliance with a reliable, well-resourced Arctic anchor. It would remove the current uncertainty about how Chinese investment in Greenlandic infrastructure would affect NATO security commitments. These are outcomes that alliance members, including Norway, Canada, and the United Kingdom, all of which have their own Arctic security concerns, would quietly welcome.

The argument that alliance solidarity requires indefinite American deference to Danish preferences on this matter conflates courtesy with strategy. The United States should conduct its pursuit diplomatically, patiently, and respectfully. It should compensate Denmark generously — not $100 million in 1946 gold prices, but something more like $50 billion in contemporary terms, accompanied by enhanced bilateral security cooperation, trade arrangements, and cultural exchange. It should do so with explicit Danish and Greenlandic participation in negotiating the terms. But it should not abandon the strategic objective simply because raising it causes diplomatic discomfort.

VI. The Climate Dimension Adds Urgency

The window for this acquisition is narrowing for reasons that have nothing to do with politics. Climate change is physically transforming Greenland in ways that are simultaneously making it more strategically valuable and more environmentally fragile. The Greenland ice sheet, which contains enough ice to raise global sea levels by approximately 24 feet if fully melted, is losing mass at an accelerating rate. This is a global catastrophe in slow motion, but it also has the short-term effect of making Greenland's territory increasingly accessible, its resources increasingly extractable, and its shipping lanes increasingly navigable.

As this process continues, the competition for Greenlandic influence will intensify. Russia and China will not wait politely for the United States and Denmark to resolve their differences. Russia has already demonstrated its willingness to make aggressive territorial claims in the Arctic — its 2007 planting of a Russian flag on the seabed at the North Pole was a theatrical gesture, but it signaled serious intent. China's growing Arctic infrastructure investments, its development of nuclear-powered icebreakers, and its explicit Arctic strategy documents all point toward a long-term commitment to Arctic presence and influence that the United States is currently positioned to counter most effectively from a sovereign foothold in Greenland.

Delay is not neutral. Every year that passes without a clear strategic commitment to Greenland is a year in which the competitive landscape shifts slightly against American interests. The time to act is before the Arctic is fully contested, not after.

VII. Addressing the Strongest Objections

Intellectual honesty requires engaging with the most powerful arguments against this position.

The self-determination objection: Greenland's people have the right to determine their own future. This is absolutely correct and should be the foundational principle of any American approach. But self-determination does not preclude Greenland choosing to associate with the United States. It precludes forcing that association. The argument here is for a negotiated, compensated, democratically endorsed transition — not for annexation. If Greenland's population, through a properly conducted referendum, chose association with the United States on genuinely fair terms, that would be an exercise of self-determination, not a violation of it.

The environmental objection: American sovereignty over Greenland would accelerate resource extraction in ways that damage the Arctic environment. This is a risk, but it is not a necessary consequence of sovereignty. The United States has the regulatory capacity to govern resource extraction responsibly, and the terms of any acquisition agreement could include explicit environmental protections and Greenlandic community consent requirements for major development projects. The alternative — Greenland's resources being developed under less regulated conditions by Chinese state-owned enterprises — is arguably a worse environmental outcome.

The precedent objection: American pursuit of Greenland would signal that wealthy nations can purchase or pressure smaller nations' territory, damaging the international rule-based order. This concern has merit, but it is moderated by two considerations. First, the acquisition would be conducted through negotiation and democratic endorsement, not military force or coercion. Second, the rule-based international order is already under serious pressure from Russia's territorial aggression and China's expansionist ambitions in the South China Sea. The relevant question is not whether the order is perfect, but whether American control of Greenland makes it more or less stable. Given the strategic benefit to the world's leading democratic power, the answer is plausibly the former.

Conclusion: Visionary Statecraft, Not Reckless Adventurism

The case for American pursuit of Greenland is not a case for bullying a small ally or disregarding the rights of an indigenous people. It is a case for clear-eyed recognition of strategic reality, conducted through the kind of patient, generous, respectful diplomacy that has characterized American territorial expansion at its best.

The Arctic is becoming the central theater of 21st-century great power competition. Greenland is the central geographic prize of the Arctic. The United States has the resources, the strategic interest, and the historical precedent to pursue this acquisition seriously. What it has lacked, until recently, is the political will to do so.

That will appears to be developing. The conversation has been opened. The task now is to conduct it seriously — not through bluster or contempt for Danish and Greenlandic sovereignty, but through the kind of sustained, well-resourced, genuinely respectful diplomatic engagement that turns a geopolitical aspiration into a strategic reality.

Seward was mocked for buying Alaska. He was right. The statesmen who ultimately secure Greenland for the United States will face similar mockery. They will also be right.

This essay presents one side of a genuinely contested strategic and ethical debate. Strong arguments exist on the other side, including concerns about Greenlandic self-determination, NATO alliance dynamics, international law, and environmental stewardship. Readers are encouraged to engage with those counterarguments as well.

The Strategic Imperative: Why the United States Must Pursue the Acquisition of Greenland

Introduction

In an era defined by great-power competition, resource scarcity, and the rapid reshaping of the global order, the United States faces a once-in-a-generation opportunity to secure its strategic future through a bold act of territorial acquisition: the purchase of Greenland from the Kingdom of Denmark. This is not a fanciful proposal rooted in imperial ambition for its own sake. It is a sober, data-driven case grounded in Arctic strategy, critical mineral sovereignty, military positioning, and the long arc of American geopolitical resilience. The arguments for this acquisition are not merely compelling — they are, upon close examination, nearly irrefutable.

I. The Arctic Is the New Center of Gravity

The Arctic is no longer a peripheral theater of geopolitics. It is rapidly becoming the fulcrum upon which global power will pivot for the remainder of the twenty-first century. As climate change accelerates the melting of polar ice, previously impassable shipping lanes are opening, vast hydrocarbon reserves are becoming accessible, and the geopolitical map of the world is being redrawn in real time.

Greenland sits at the absolute center of this transformation. Its geographic position at the mouth of the Northwest Passage and along the GIUK Gap — the strategic corridor between Greenland, Iceland, and the United Kingdom — gives whoever controls it an unmatched vantage point over the North Atlantic and the Arctic Ocean. No other single territory on Earth offers such a commanding position over the emerging maritime highways of the north.

Russia has understood this for decades. Moscow has invested tens of billions of dollars in Arctic military infrastructure, reopened Cold War–era bases, and deployed advanced missile systems along its northern coast. China, despite having no territorial claim to the Arctic, has declared itself a "near-Arctic state" and is funneling billions into Arctic research, shipping partnerships, and resource extraction ventures. These are not abstract posturings. They are concrete moves in a geopolitical chess game that the United States cannot afford to watch from the sidelines.

Owning Greenland would place American military assets, surveillance systems, and naval infrastructure at the very heart of the Arctic theater. It would give the United States permanent, sovereign control over the most strategically significant landmass in the northern hemisphere — a landmass that Denmark, for all its admirable governance, simply does not have the military or economic capacity to develop or defend at the scale the moment demands.

II. Critical Minerals and Resource Sovereignty

Perhaps the most urgent and tangible argument for acquiring Greenland is its extraordinary wealth of critical minerals. Greenland's geological profile contains deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, zinc, iron, copper, gold, and — crucially — the raw materials essential to the technologies that will define the next century: electric vehicle batteries, advanced semiconductors, wind turbines, fighter jets, and precision-guided munitions.

The numbers are staggering. Estimates suggest Greenland holds approximately 38.5 million metric tons of rare earth oxides, making it one of the largest repositories of these elements outside of China. To put this in context, China currently controls roughly 60 to 70 percent of global rare earth mining and an even larger share of rare earth processing. This monopoly gives Beijing extraordinary leverage over the supply chains that underpin American technological and military competitiveness. Every semiconductor fab in Arizona, every F-35 production line, every electric vehicle assembly plant in Michigan depends, in some measure, on minerals that flow through Chinese-controlled supply chains.

Greenland represents a geopolitical circuit-breaker. If the United States acquired Greenland, it could develop these mineral deposits under American regulatory and environmental standards, creating a Western-controlled alternative to Chinese rare earth dominance. The Kvanefjeld deposit alone is estimated to contain one of the world's largest deposits of rare earth elements alongside significant uranium reserves. The Zackenberg and other sites add further depth to the territory's resource portfolio.

Critics will argue that extraction is expensive and environmentally challenging. This is true. But the strategic calculus is not about profit margins in the next fiscal quarter. It is about ensuring that, thirty years from now, the United States and its allies are not held hostage by a single foreign power for the raw materials of modern civilization. The cost of acquiring Greenland, even at the widely cited figure of several hundred billion dollars, would be a fraction of the long-term economic and strategic cost of continued rare earth dependency on Beijing.

III. Military and Defense Strategy

The defense case for Greenland is rooted in a strategic reality that has been understood since the Cold War but has only grown more urgent: whoever controls Greenland controls the northern flank of the Western world.

During World War II, the United States recognized this principle when it occupied Greenland to prevent it from falling under Nazi control — an occupation that Denmark, then under German occupation itself, tacitly accepted. After the war, the United States and Denmark signed the 1951 Defense Agreement, which gave Washington the right to build and operate military bases on the island. The result was Thule Air Base (now Pituffik Space Base), one of the most important military installations in the Western Hemisphere.

Pituffik serves as a critical node in the United States' missile warning and satellite tracking architecture. It is the northernmost deep-water port in the world, a key installation for the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), and a cornerstone of early warning systems against intercontinental ballistic missiles launched over the pole. Its strategic value is, in a very literal sense, incalculable.

Yet the current arrangement is fragile. The United States operates on Danish sovereignty, meaning that its access to and use of the base is subject to the political dynamics of a foreign government. Denmark's recent decision to modernize its Arctic defense posture — prompted in part by Trump's initial interest in 2019 — is commendable, but it does not change the fundamental asymmetry: Denmark's entire defense budget is approximately $5 billion per year. The United States' is over $800 billion. When it comes to defending the Arctic against Russian and Chinese encroachment, the scale of commitment simply does not match.

Full American sovereignty over Greenland would allow the United States to build a comprehensive military infrastructure across the island without diplomatic friction or political uncertainty. It would permit the construction of new air bases, deep-water ports for icebreaker fleets, expanded early warning systems, and permanent Arctic training facilities. It would also allow the integration of Greenland into a unified Arctic defense network alongside Alaska and northern Canada.

IV. The Historical and Legal Precedent

The acquisition of territory through purchase is not an aberration in American history. It is a defining feature of it.

In 1803, the United States purchased the Louisiana Territory from France for approximately $15 million, doubling the size of the nation overnight. In 1867, Secretary of State William Seward acquired Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million — a transaction so widely mocked that the territory was derisively called "Seward's Folly." History, of course, vindicated the purchase: Alaska's gold, oil, fisheries, and strategic military value have returned that initial investment billions of times over.

More recently, the United States has purchased sovereign territory from Denmark before. In 1917, Washington bought the Danish West Indies for $25 million, creating the U.S. Virgin Islands. The transaction was peaceful, mutually agreed upon, and straightforward in its legal architecture. There is nothing in international law, Danish constitutional law, or the self-determination principles of the Greenlandic people that would prevent a similar arrangement from being negotiated today.

Greenland already enjoys a high degree of self-governance under the Danish realm. The Self-Government Act of 2009 established that the people of Greenland may, at any time, vote to become fully independent. The question of sovereignty is, in the most fundamental sense, already on the table. What is being proposed here is not the overthrow of a people's will but the negotiation of a mutually beneficial arrangement in which Greenland's residents would become citizens of the wealthiest and most powerful nation on Earth, with access to American infrastructure investment, educational opportunities, healthcare systems, and economic development at a scale that Denmark — however well-intentioned — cannot match.

V. Economic Development and the Greenlandic People

The current relationship between Greenland and Denmark, while respectful, is not without tension. Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people receives a substantial annual subsidy from Copenhagen — approximately $600 million per year, or roughly one-third of the island's GDP. This subsidy underwrites public services, infrastructure, and the Greenlandic government's operating budget. But it also creates a structural dependency that limits Greenland's economic autonomy and ambitions.

An American acquisition would not merely replace one sovereign patron with another. It would fundamentally alter Greenland's economic trajectory. The United States could invest tens of billions of dollars in mining infrastructure, transportation networks, renewable energy projects, and digital connectivity. It could transform the island from a territory sustained by a Nordic welfare subsidy into a self-sustaining economic powerhouse fueled by the very resources that the rest of the world desperately needs.

Consider what happened after the Louisiana Purchase. The territory was developed, settled, and integrated into the American economy in ways that no French colonial administration ever envisioned. The same logic applies to Alaska, which went from a sparsely populated fur-trading outpost to a major economic contributor producing over 500 million barrels of oil annually at its peak.

Greenland's residents would, under American sovereignty, gain the full rights and protections of U.S. citizenship. They would have access to the largest economy on Earth, the most extensive federal infrastructure programs, and the legal and constitutional frameworks that have attracted immigrants for over two centuries. The Greenlandic Inuit population, whose culture and identity are central to the island's character, would have the institutional backing of a nation that has increasingly committed itself to the rights and recognition of indigenous peoples.

VI. Preempting Strategic Adversaries

There is one argument that trumps all others in its urgency: if the United States does not secure Greenland, someone else will — or, more precisely, someone else will secure the influence that matters.

China has already made overtures to Greenland. In 2018, Beijing proposed a $5.5 billion investment in Greenland's mining and airport infrastructure. The Danish government, responding to pressure from Washington, blocked the deal. But the attempt revealed a critical vulnerability: Greenland's infrastructure and development needs are enormous, and Denmark cannot always meet them. If the United States does not step in with a comprehensive, sovereign commitment, China will find other ways to extend its influence — through commercial partnerships, resource agreements, or investments that come with strategic strings attached.

Russia, for its part, does not need to acquire Greenland to benefit from Western inattention to the Arctic. Every year that the United States delays a comprehensive Arctic strategy is a year in which Russia expands its military footprint, controls more shipping traffic, and entrenches its position as the dominant Arctic power.

The window for action is not infinite. As climate change accelerates, the economic and military value of the Arctic will only increase, and the price of acquisition — whether measured in dollars, diplomatic capital, or political will — will only rise. The United States has the means, the precedent, and the strategic necessity to act. What it has lacked, until recently, is the political imagination.

Conclusion

The acquisition of Greenland is not a whimsical fantasy. It is a strategic imperative that sits at the intersection of military security, resource sovereignty, economic development, and great-power competition. It has deep historical precedent in American statecraft. It would benefit not only the United States but the people of Greenland themselves, who would gain access to unprecedented economic investment and the protections of American citizenship. It would preempt the ambitions of strategic adversaries who are already circling. And it would secure the most strategically significant territory in the Arctic at a moment when control of the Arctic is rapidly becoming the defining geopolitical contest of the century.

The United States has always been a nation that thought big — that saw opportunities where others saw risk, and acted when hesitation would have meant decline. The acquisition of Greenland is the next chapter in that story. The question is not whether America can afford to pursue it. The question is whether America can afford not to.

Note: This essay was written as a persuasive argument from a particular geopolitical perspective. Real-world acquisition of Greenland would involve complex questions of international law, indigenous sovereignty, environmental stewardship, and the expressed wishes of the Greenlandic people themselves — factors that deserve serious and ongoing deliberation beyond the scope of this persuasive exercise.
